title: Signing of the Charter of the United Nations
summary: On 26 June 1945, delegates of 50 states signed the Charter of the United Nations in San Francisco, ending a two-month conference. It created the UN, a Security Council with five veto-holding permanent members, and a trusteeship system; it took effect on 24 October 1945.
card: After the Allied governments drafted proposals at Dumbarton Oaks and Yalta, 850 delegates from 50 countries met in San Francisco from 25 April 1945 and signed the Charter on 26 June. Smaller states challenged the great-power veto and lost, while a handful of women delegates and some small states won language on equal rights and human rights. The Charter took effect on 24 October 1945, once China, France, the USSR, the UK, the US and a majority of other signatories had ratified.
what:
The Charter of the United Nations is the founding treaty of the world organisation that succeeded the League of Nations. Its design was worked out by the United States, United Kingdom, Soviet Union and China at Dumbarton Oaks in Washington (21 August to 7 October 1944), and the Security Council voting rule was settled at the Yalta Conference (4 to 11 February 1945). The United Nations Conference on International Organization then met in San Francisco from 25 April 1945; about 850 delegates from 50 countries took part, according to the National WWII Museum. The plenary session approved the Charter unanimously on 25 June, and it was signed the next day in the Herbst Theatre of the Veterans Building, with a space left for Poland, which had no agreed government to send. Poland signed afterwards, which is why the original members are counted as 51.

The Charter set out six principal organs: a General Assembly in which every member has one vote, a Security Council, an Economic and Social Council, a Trusteeship Council, an International Court of Justice and a Secretariat. Its purposes include maintaining peace and security, friendly relations based on equal rights and self-determination of peoples, and international cooperation in promoting human rights. Article 2(7) bars the UN from intervening in matters essentially within a state's domestic jurisdiction, and Chapter XI commits states administering colonies to treat the inhabitants' interests as paramount.

The central controversy was the veto. Smaller states, led in debate by Australia's Herbert Evatt, argued that permanent seats and a veto contradicted sovereign equality; the sponsoring governments replied that without the veto there would be no organisation, and the committee approved it on 20 June by 30 votes to 2 with 15 abstentions, per Robert James's 2023 study. The Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945 when the five permanent members and a majority of the other signatories had deposited ratifications. Accounts differ on the number of signatories: a UN history gives 160 signatories, while the U.S. State Department's compilation counts 153 delegates signing on 26 June, a gap that may reflect how multiple signatories per country are counted.

uncertainty.note: The record spans the conference opening (25 April 1945) to entry into force (24 October 1945). The signing itself, 26 June 1945, is the event named in the id; the plenary approval was 25 June. Poland signed after 26 June.

how: The Charter was built in three stages. At Dumbarton Oaks in 1944 the four sponsoring governments drafted a structure of Assembly, Council, court and secretariat. At Yalta in February 1945 the Allied leaders settled how the Security Council would vote, and called the San Francisco conference. At San Francisco the sponsors accepted many amendments on rights, economic cooperation and trusteeship while refusing to alter the veto. On 22 May the smaller states submitted a questionnaire on the voting rule; the Soviet side then briefly insisted that even discussing a dispute needed unanimity, a deadlock broken when Stalin yielded to Harry Hopkins in Moscow on 6 June. The sponsors issued a joint statement on 8 June reaffirming the veto, and the committee approved it on 20 June. Plenary approval followed on 25 June and signature on 26 June. Under Article 110 each state ratified by its own procedure, depositing instruments with the United States government. The U.S. Senate consented on 28 July by 89 votes to 2, and the Charter took effect on 24 October 1945.
why_it_matters:
The Charter turned wartime alliance into a standing institution that nearly every state has since joined. Its Security Council gave the post-1945 order a legal frame for sanctions, peacekeeping and authorised use of force, and its human rights language, pressed by a handful of women delegates and by small Latin American states, led to a Commission on the Status of Women within a year. Chapters XI to XIII committed colonial powers to treat the interests of dependent peoples as paramount, to report on their territories and to place some under trusteeship, giving anti-colonial movements an international forum the League had not offered, though British and French colonies were largely left out of trusteeship.

The veto has had lasting costs. Because a permanent member can block any substantive decision, the Council can be paralysed on conflicts involving one of the five or their allies, and reform proposals have not advanced in eight decades. Article 2(7) likewise shielded states from outside scrutiny of their internal conduct.

Counterfactually, had the smaller states won, the sponsors said they would not join; Stettinius judged that if Stalin had held to Molotov's position there would have been no United Nations at San Francisco. The organisation might then have repeated the League's weakness or never been founded. The permanent seats of China, France, the USSR (now Russia), the UK and the US, fixed in 1945, still shape every UN negotiation today.

perspectives.holder: Smaller and middle powers (Australia, New Zealand and others)
perspectives.account: Permanent seats and a unanimity rule contradicted the sovereign equality proclaimed in wartime declarations; on 22 May 1945 they submitted a questionnaire on the voting rule, and Evatt objected chiefly to a veto over discussion rather than over enforcement.

perspectives.holder: The sponsoring great powers (United States, United Kingdom, USSR, China)
perspectives.account: The Council could act only with the willing military support of the major powers, so unanimity among them was required; US senators said the Senate would not have consented without it, and Connally told delegates that rejecting the veto meant no Charter.

perspectives.holder: Colonised peoples and the colonial powers
perspectives.account: Chapter XI declared the interests of dependent peoples paramount and created reporting duties, but trusteeship covered only mandates, former Axis colonies and voluntarily placed territories, and British and French colonies were not folded in. The peoples concerned had few voices at the conference. In 1946 eight administering states submitted lists of territories under Article 73e.
